1394.title: Pilgrimage: Sarnath
1394.hook: the Deer Park where the first sermon was given
1394.howItsDone: Pilgrims visit Sarnath near Varanasi to walk around the great stupa, see the ruins of ancient monasteries, and chant or listen to the discourse on setting the wheel of the teaching in motion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bodh Gaya: a tower, a tree, and many schools in one shade. Your line was where he woke. The four truths first came on day 4, without jargon; today, the park where they were first spoken.

Five men are sitting in a park near the city of Benares when they see someone walking toward them on the road. They know him. He used to fast and strain alongside them, and then he quit and started eating again. They decided he'd gone soft. So they make a pact: when he gets here, nobody stands up. Nobody takes his bowl. Maybe offer him a seat, if he insists. Then he comes closer, and something about the way he walks undoes the whole plan. One takes his robe. Another sets out water. Someone offers a seat. The park was full of deer, and the talk he gave there is why pilgrims still come.
screen: `FIVE OLD FRIENDS MAKE A PACT.` → `NOBODY STANDS UP.` → `EVERYBODY STANDS UP.`

segments.voice: First, the place. The texts call it Isipatana, the deer park near Benares. Today it's Sarnath, a quiet green with the ruins of old monasteries and a great round stupa of brick and stone. Pilgrims walk around it; some sit on the grass and listen to the teaching read aloud. Second, the talk, called Setting in Motion the Wheel of the Teaching. It opens not with doctrine but with a warning about two dead ends: chasing pleasure, and punishing the body. The Buddha had tried both. Between them, he says, is a middle way, and it leads to peace and to awakening. Third, the four truths. There is suffering. It has a cause, the craving that keeps reaching for more. It can end. And there is a path to its ending. Here's the detail worth keeping: in the discourse, each truth comes with a job. Suffering is to be understood. Craving is to be let go. The ending is to be realized. The path is to be walked. Not four statements to agree with: four tasks. Fourth, the moment it lands. As the Buddha speaks, one of the five, Kondanna, sees it for himself: whatever arises also passes away. The Buddha says, Kondanna has understood. And the text says the gods shout the news from one heaven to the next: at Benares, in the deer park, the wheel has been set rolling.
screen: `ISIPATANA, THE DEER PARK.` · `NEITHER PLEASURE NOR PUNISHMENT.` · `FOUR TRUTHS, FOUR TASKS.` · then, large: `THE WHEEL SET ROLLING.`

segments.voice: Breathe out, then say the four truths quietly, one per breath: there is suffering, there is a cause of suffering, there is an end of suffering, there is a path. Say them again with each task under your breath: understand, let go, realize, walk. Then let the words go and breathe, on the grass with the deer.
Pilgrimage. The road to the holy places. Its third stop is Sarnath, the deer park where the Buddha set the wheel of the teaching rolling. Today's word.
Your line: where he taught. Four truths, and each one a task. I'll be here tomorrow.

1395.title: Pilgrimage: Kushinagar
1395.hook: the place of the passing, with a great reclining Buddha
1395.howItsDone: Pilgrims visit Kushinagar in India, walk around the reclining Buddha in the Mahaparinirvana temple, offer robes and flowers, and visit the stupa honored as the place of the cremation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sarnath: the deer park, four truths and four tasks. Your line was where he taught. Day 84 told his last words; today, the place where he spoke them.

The statue is long, golden, and lying down. Inside a white temple in a small town in northern India, the Buddha rests on his right side, head propped on his hand, eyes almost closed, feet neatly together. Pilgrims walk slowly around him. Some lay a length of saffron cloth over the body, the way you might tuck a blanket around someone you love. A few people cry; others sit by the wall and chant. Visitors sometimes take it for the Buddha napping. It isn't. It shows the last hours of his life. This is Kushinagar, the fourth place the Buddha named as worth a pilgrim's visit.
screen: `A GOLDEN BUDDHA, LYING DOWN.` → `NOT SLEEPING.` → `THE LAST HOURS.`

segments.voice: The Great Discourse on the Final Passing tells it slowly. First, the posture. Old and ill, the Buddha asks Ananda to set out a couch between twin sal trees, head to the north. He lies on his right side, one foot on the other, mindful and clear. The text calls it the lion's posture. The trees, it says, burst into bloom out of season and drop their flowers on him. Second, the grief. Ananda goes off alone and weeps. The Buddha sends for him and gently reminds him of what he has always taught: everything dear to us is one day parted from us. Then he praises Ananda's years of kindness in front of everyone. Third, a latecomer. A wanderer named Subhadda arrives with a question, and Ananda tries to turn him away: do not trouble the teacher, he is weary. The Buddha overhears, lets him in, and teaches him. Even at the end, the door stays open. Fourth, the last words. He asks the monks, again and again, whether anyone has a doubt left. No one speaks. And then, in Rhys Davids's old translation: "Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!" Buddhists call what followed the parinibbana, the final passing. Pilgrims come to Kushinagar not only to mourn, but to sit near the place where the teacher, dying, kept teaching.
screen: `ON HIS RIGHT SIDE, LIKE A LION.` · `ANANDA WEEPS.` · `THE DOOR STAYS OPEN.` · then, large: `WORK OUT YOUR SALVATION WITH DILIGENCE.`

segments.voice: If your body and space allow, lie on your right side for a minute, one foot resting on the other, head on your hand or a pillow; if not, lean a little to the right in your chair. Breathe slowly, calm rather than sad, and remember the trees dropping flowers and the teacher who used his last strength to answer one more question. When you're ready, sit up slowly.
Pilgrimage. Walking to remember. Its fourth great stop is Kushinagar, where the Buddha passed away between the sal trees. Today's word.
Your line: where he passed. Even dying, he kept the door open for one more question. Until tomorrow.

fork.reveal: Ananda turned him away, kindly. but the Buddha overheard, called Subhadda in, and taught him. even at the end, the door stayed open.

original.note: Pali parinibbana: the final passing of the Buddha.

1396.title: Pilgrimage: Vulture Peak
1396.hook: the hill at Rajgir where many Mahayana sutras are set
1396.howItsDone: Pilgrims climb the stone path to Vulture Peak near Rajgir, often before dawn, and chant sutras, offer lamps and flowers, or sit in meditation on the brick platform at the top.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kushinagar: the reclining Buddha and the twin sal trees. Your line was where he passed. Day 545 began this discourse with a king's question; today, the hill where it was asked.

The path is stone, and it goes up. In the dark before sunrise, pilgrims climb it with flashlights, past boulders and scrub, breathing hard, stopping at small caves. At the top there is no great temple: a low brick platform on a rocky ledge, a few lamps, some flowers, and a wide view over green hills just as the sky lightens. Someone opens a small book and starts to chant, and the people around join in, low, against the wind. The hill is near the town of Rajgir in India, and in the old texts it has a strange name.
screen: `A STONE PATH IN THE DARK.` → `A BRICK LEDGE AT THE TOP.` → `CHANTING AT DAWN.`

segments.voice: First, the name. In Pali it's Gijjhakuta, vulture peak; some say the rocks at the top look like a vulture, folded and watching. In the Buddha's day the town below was Rajagaha, a royal city, and the texts place him on this hill. Second, the old discourses. The Great Discourse on the Final Passing, the one followed to Kushinagar yesterday, opens right here. A king sends his chief minister up the path to ask the Buddha about going to war. The Buddha answers by talking about what keeps a people strong: meeting often, living in harmony, honoring their elders. A hill for hard questions. Third, the Mahayana sutras. For Mahayana Buddhists, this hill is where the Buddha gave some of the teachings they treasure. The Lotus Sutra opens on Vulture Peak, with a vast assembly gathered, and the longer form of the Heart Sutra is set here too. So when Mahayana pilgrims chant at the top, they chant words that, in their tradition, were first heard on this very ledge. Fourth, a story Zen tells. On Vulture Peak, it says, the Buddha once held up a flower and said nothing. Only one disciple, Mahakashyapa, smiled. Zen traces its line of teachers back to that smile. The story is told in later Chinese Zen collections, such as the Gateless Gate, and Zen tells it as its own beginning. One hill holds the old discourses, the great Mahayana sutras, and a wordless flower.
screen: `GIJJHAKUTA, VULTURE PEAK.` · `A KING'S QUESTION ABOUT WAR.` · `WHERE THE LOTUS SUTRA OPENS.` · then, large: `A FLOWER AND A SMILE.`

segments.voice: If stairs are near and your body is up for it, climb a few slowly, feeling each foot lift, move and land; if not, lift each foot slowly in place while seated. At the top, stop and stand still as if a view were opening in front of you, then sit and let your breath settle.
Pilgrimage. Going to the place to remember what happened there. On Vulture Peak, pilgrims climb to the ledge where the texts say the Buddha stayed and taught. Today's word.
Your line: the hill of sutras. One ledge, and three ways of remembering it. Go gently.

1397.title: Two traveling together
1397.hook: the Shikoku pilgrimage around Kukai's island, walked by pilgrims in white
1397.carry: two traveling together: kukai walks with the pilgrim
1397.howItsDone: Pilgrims on Shikoku, often dressed in white with a hat and staff, visit the temples of the circuit on foot, by bus or by car, chanting at each one and collecting a red seal in a pilgrim's book, while islanders offer them small gifts called osettai.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vulture Peak: a ledge at dawn and a flower held up in silence. Your line was the hill of sutras.

On a country road in Japan, an old woman steps out of her house and holds out an orange to a stranger. The stranger is dressed all in white, with a wide sedge hat, a wooden staff, and a little bell that rings with each step. The stranger bows, takes the orange, and walks on. The woman goes back inside. Neither of them thinks this is odd. On this island, people in white have been walking past front doors like hers for a very long time, on a road that goes all the way around and comes back to where it started. The island is Shikoku.
screen: `AN ORANGE ON A COUNTRY ROAD.` → `A PILGRIM IN WHITE.` → `A ROAD THAT COMES BACK AROUND.`

segments.voice: First, the teacher behind the road. Kukai, also known as Kobo Daishi, is the teacher tradition credits with bringing the esoteric teaching called Shingon to Japan, and Shikoku is the island tradition calls his home. The pilgrimage follows temples linked with him, in a great loop around the island. The pilgrim is called a henro. Second, the clothes. The white jacket is the mark of a pilgrim. Some say white was chosen because it's the color of burial clothes, so a pilgrim sets out ready for anything the road brings. The staff, tradition says, stands for Kukai himself. Third, two on the road. Some pilgrims' hats carry words that mean two traveling together: the pilgrim may walk alone, but the teaching says Kukai walks beside them the whole way. So at night, tradition says, pilgrims wash the tip of the staff before their own feet, caring for their companion first. And at each temple, a pilgrim chants, leaves a slip with their name, and has a book stamped with a red seal and brushed with ink. Fourth, the people along the way. Islanders offer pilgrims small gifts, an orange, tea, a ride, a bed. It's called osettai, and the pilgrim receives it as given to Kukai, not to themselves. Some walk the whole loop at once. Others come back a section at a time, over years. Some go by bus or car. However they go, the road brings them back to the temple where they began. A circle, not a line.
screen: `KUKAI'S ISLAND.` · `WHITE CLOTHES, A STAFF, A HAT.` · `TWO TRAVELING TOGETHER.` · then, large: `A CIRCLE, NOT A LINE.`

segments.voice: If your space allows, choose a little circle, around a room, a table or a yard, and walk it slowly with an easy breath, letting whoever you hold dear walk beside you, like the two traveling together. When you come back to where you started, stop and bow, or simply stand still. If walking isn't possible, trace a slow circle with your hand.
Eighty-eight temples. The pilgrimage around Shikoku, Kukai's island, walked by pilgrims in white who, tradition says, never walk alone. Today's word.
Your line: two traveling together. Kukai walks with every pilgrim, and the circle comes back home. See you tomorrow.

1398.title: The circle around Kailash
1398.hook: the pilgrimage around Mount Kailash, sacred to several traditions
1398.carry: circle the holy, keeping it on your right
1398.howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhist pilgrims walk the kora around Mount Kailash clockwise, some making full-body prostrations along the way, and Buddhists also circle stupas and temples clockwise as a sign of respect.

segments.voice: Yesterday, eighty-eight temples: pilgrims in white circling Kukai's island, an orange held out on a country road. Your line was two traveling together.

Snow on a black pyramid of rock, alone above a high, bare plateau in western Tibet. Pilgrims don't walk up it. They walk around it. A family walks together, the youngest riding on a father's shoulders. A young man lies flat on the stony path, stretches his arms forward, marks the spot, stands, steps to the mark, and lies down again, measuring the whole circle with his body. A group of pilgrims from India moves past, chanting a different name for the same mountain. Now and then, someone comes the other way, walking the circle in the opposite direction. The mountain is Kailash.
screen: `SNOW ON A BLACK PEAK.` → `PILGRIMS DON'T CLIMB IT.` → `THEY WALK AROUND IT.`

segments.voice: First, a very old gesture. Walking around something holy, keeping it on your right, is a way Buddhists show respect, and it goes back to the texts. Again and again in the old discourses, someone who has listened to the Buddha rises, bows, and departs keeping him on the right. So circling a stupa, a temple or a mountain clockwise carries that same bow forward, step by step. Second, the mountain. For Tibetan Buddhists, Kailash is the home of a great meditation deity, and the circle around it, called a kora, is a pilgrimage they hold dear. The path climbs to a high pass, where pilgrims hang prayer flags and some leave a small thing of their own, a bit of cloth, a lock of hair, as a sign of leaving the old life on the mountain. Third, the neighbors. Kailash is not only a Buddhist mountain. Hindus honor it as the dwelling of Shiva. Jains revere it as a place of liberation. Followers of Bon, the old religion of Tibet, hold it sacred too, and they walk the circle counterclockwise, by their own custom. So people of several faiths pass one another on the same path, each for their own reasons, and nobody has to agree to share the trail. Fourth, why around and not up. Tradition holds the summit is not to be climbed. The center stays untouched. The pilgrimage is the circle.
screen: `KEEPING IT ON THE RIGHT.` · `THE KORA AND THE HIGH PASS.` · `SEVERAL FAITHS, ONE TRAIL.` · then, large: `THE CENTER STAYS UNTOUCHED.`

segments.voice: Choose a center, a plant, a candle, a chair, an image that means something to you, and walk slowly around it clockwise, keeping it on your right, once or a few times; if you can't walk, trace the circle with your eyes. Then stop facing the center and stay with it a moment. You don't need to reach it; you're circling it.
Around the mountain. The kora around Mount Kailash, walked by Buddhists and by people of several other faiths, circling a peak that tradition says is not to be climbed. Today's word.
Your line: circle the holy, keeping it on your right. The center stays untouched, and many faiths share the trail. That's today, done.

1399.title: Giving as practice
1399.hook: the first perfection lived: give something daily this week
1399.howItsDone: Buddhists practice dana by offering food to monks and nuns, supporting temples, and giving to people in need, and in Theravada countries the morning alms round is a daily chance to give.

segments.voice: Yesterday, around the mountain: Kailash, a kora, and a summit left unclimbed. Your line was around the mountain. Dana first came up on day 5; now, giving as a practice of its own.

A bowl of rice is passed from hand to hand at dawn. A monk walks barefoot down a street, someone kneels and spoons food into his bowl, and the monk says nothing and walks on. Neither one says thank you. That isn't rudeness. The giver isn't doing the monk a favor, and the monk isn't doing the giver one either. After a week walking to the places of the Buddha's life, the path turns inward, to the perfections, the qualities Buddhists say a person grows on the way to awakening. The list begins with the simplest thing in that bowl.
screen: `RICE INTO A BOWL AT DAWN.` → `NO THANK YOU, AND NO FAVOR.` → `THE PERFECTIONS BEGIN.`

segments.voice: First, the list. Theravada Buddhists keep one list of perfections and Mahayana Buddhists keep another, differing in length and wording. But both begin in the same place: giving, dana. Before anything else on either list, the open hand. Second, the Buddha's own claim. In a short collection called the Itivuttaka, he says something startling. If people knew, as he knows, the fruit of giving and sharing, they would not eat without giving first. Even their last bite, their last mouthful, they would not eat without sharing, if there were someone to share it with. Not the leftovers: the last mouthful. Third, two kinds of gift. In the same collection, the Buddha names the gift of material things and the gift of the teaching. Bread is a gift. So is a true word at the right time. Neither needs to be large. Fourth, why it's a practice and not just a kind act. Giving loosens the grip. A verse of the Dhammapada, in Max Muller's old translation, puts it this way: "Let a man overcome anger by love, let him overcome evil by good; let him overcome the greedy by liberality, the liar by truth!" Liberality is the old word for generosity, and here it's a medicine for grasping, including one's own. So giving, to monks, neighbors, strangers, isn't only to help, though it helps. It's a way to practice letting go, one small thing at a time. That's why nobody needs to say thank you at the bowl. The giving was the practice.

1400.title: Ethics as practice
1400.hook: the second perfection: keep your precepts as a gift
1400.howItsDone: Lay Buddhists take or renew the five precepts by reciting them in Pali or in their own language, at the temple or at home, and some keep additional precepts on observance days.

segments.voice: Yesterday, giving as practice: rice into a bowl, and even the last mouthful shared. Your line was the first perfection. The precepts first came on day 12, five that read like kindness; today, they're gifts.

A rule is usually something you keep for your own sake, or to stay out of trouble. Don't speed, and you won't get a ticket. Don't lie, and you won't get caught. Now turn that around. What if every rule you kept were a present you handed to someone else? Not to the police, not to a teacher, but to the stranger on the sidewalk, the person in the next apartment, the animal in the yard. That's the startling turn the Buddha gives to ethics. The perfections began with giving. The second, ethics, turns out to be giving too, only quieter.
screen: `A RULE KEPT FOR YOUR OWN SAKE.` → `TURN IT AROUND.` → `A PRESENT TO A STRANGER.`

segments.voice: First, the word. In Pali it's sila: ethics, good conduct, the way you live with others. It comes second in both lists of perfections, right after giving. For lay Buddhists, it's shaped by the five precepts: not killing, not stealing, no sexual misconduct, no false speech, and no intoxicants that cloud the mind. Second, the surprise. In a discourse in the Numerical Discourses, the Buddha calls these precepts five gifts. Keeping the first, not to kill, gives beings freedom from fear, freedom from hostility, freedom from harm. The text says this gift reaches beings without limit, and the giver shares in the same freedom. Nobody near you has to wonder whether you'll hurt them. That's a gift, even if no one ever knows you gave it. Third, the heart of the teaching. A verse of the Dhammapada, in Max Muller's old translation, sums it up: "Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind, that is the teaching of (all) the Awakened." Notice the order: stop harming first, then do good, then the mind. Ethics is the ground the rest stands on. Fourth, keeping them again. The precepts aren't vows taken once and forgotten. In temples and homes, they're recited again and taken up afresh. A slip isn't the end; it's a reason to begin again tomorrow. After a week walking to Sarnath, Kushinagar and Vulture Peak, around an island and a mountain, the road turns out to be under your own feet.

segments.voice: Let the breath settle, then choose one precept, not harming, not taking, honest speech, care with your body, or a clear mind, and say it quietly in your own words as something you intend for one day. Bring to mind the people and creatures you'll pass today as the ones receiving it. They'll never know; it's still a gift.
Ethics as practice. Sila, the second perfection: keeping the precepts carefully, as a gift of safety and freedom from fear to everyone around you. Today's word.
Your line: the second perfection. Freedom from fear, handed quietly to strangers. See you tomorrow.
